title: "Research"

::: {.research-intro}
My research aims to understand and model dynamic land-surface processes from heterogeneous Earth observation data. During my master's study, my research focused on process-based crop growth modelling, which provided me with a physical understanding of soil–plant–atmosphere interactions and how land-surface states evolve in response to environmental drivers.

During my PhD, I shifted toward high-resolution crop yield prediction using Earth observation data. A central challenge was the scarcity of high-resolution crop yield labels: producing 10 m yield maps across Heilongjiang Province had to rely on only around 5,000 sparse and noisy field samples. This limitation led me to investigate how robust representations could be learned with much weaker supervision. I first explored multi-task learning, using related agricultural tasks to provide complementary supervision, and subsequently turned to self-supervised learning from large volumes of unlabeled remote sensing observations.

This progression gradually shifted my research focus from crop yield prediction itself to spatiotemporal representation learning for Earth observation. My current research focuses on developing dynamic representations of land-surface states from heterogeneous, asynchronous, and incomplete observations to support downstream agricultural applications.
:::

## Multi-source Crop Yield Prediction

### What information is available for prediction?

This stage established a controlled benchmark for understanding which data sources and modelling choices matter as crop-yield prediction expands across crops, regions, and years.

<details class="research-details">
<summary>How this research developed</summary>
<div class="research-details-body">
<h4>Origin</h4>
<p>This line of research began in March 2023, when I had just begun exploring high-resolution crop yield prediction while developing models for an enterprise partner. Most studies I encountered followed a similar paradigm, combining machine-learning models with predictors derived from remote sensing, meteorological, soil, and other environmental data. During technical route selection, two fundamental questions emerged: should a separate model be trained for each crop, or can multiple crops be modelled jointly? Similarly, should models be developed separately for individual regions, or can data from multiple regions be combined within a unified model? These practical questions led to a broader research question: as crop-yield prediction expands from individual crops and regions to heterogeneous agricultural systems, which modelling choices actually determine predictive performance?</p>
<h4>Benchmark</h4>
<p>To address the lack of systematic evidence, I developed a unified machine-learning benchmark for multi-crop yield prediction. Under consistent data splits and evaluation protocols, it examined joint versus crop-specific modelling, absolute versus normalized yield targets, the availability of crop identity, combinations of remote-sensing, meteorological, soil, and terrain variables, seasonal observation windows, and cross-year transfer. Multiple tree-based algorithms were evaluated under the same conditions, allowing the effects of modelling choices to be distinguished from differences among algorithms.</p>
<h4>Key finding</h4>
<p>The experiments showed that <strong>reliable crop identity was more important than the choice among the evaluated machine-learning algorithms</strong>. Although crop classification achieved relatively high accuracy, its errors propagated into the subsequent yield-regression stage and caused substantial performance degradation. The results also confirmed the importance of remote-sensing and meteorological information and demonstrated the feasibility of predicting yield before the end of the growing season.</p>
<h4>Research transition</h4>
<p>This work provided an empirical foundation for my subsequent research. It reinforced the importance of integrating multi-source observations, exposed the limitations of pipelines that require crop identity as an explicit input, and showed that tabular models cannot directly exploit spatial context. These observations motivated my transition toward end-to-end spatial learning and multi-task representation learning.</p>
</div>
</details>

## Learning with Limited Labels

### How can spatial detail be learned when labels are scarce?

This stage investigated how auxiliary supervision and shared spatial representations can support pixel-level yield prediction when dense yield labels are scarce.

<details class="research-details">
<summary>How this research developed</summary>
<div class="research-details-body">
<h4>Starting question</h4>
<p>In October 2023, this line of research began with a simple question: <strong>dense-prediction architectures such as U-Net had become highly effective for pixel-level prediction in remote sensing, yet they had rarely been applied to pixel-level crop-yield prediction. Why?</strong> I came to believe that the main obstacle was not the architecture itself, but the scarcity of reliable, spatially dense yield labels.</p>
<h4>Reframing the problem</h4>
<p>I initially explored clustering-based data augmentation and loss functions designed for long-tailed yield distributions. Subsequent experiments showed that clustering-based augmentation introduced additional label noise and further exacerbated the long-tailed distribution. This led me to reframe the problem: the central limitation was not how to compensate for scarce data through augmentation or loss design, but how to provide sufficient supervisory signals for learning meaningful representations. I therefore developed <strong>MT-CYP-Net</strong>, a multi-task framework that jointly models crop classification and yield prediction. Crop-type supervision complements scarce yield labels through shared representations, improving learning under limited training data.</p>
<h4>Research transition</h4>
<p>This work demonstrated the value of auxiliary supervision, while also revealing a more fundamental limitation of supervised learning: representations remain constrained by the availability and quality of task-specific labels. This realization motivated my subsequent turn toward self-supervised learning from large volumes of unlabeled Earth observation data.</p>
</div>
</details>

## Multimodal Spatiotemporal Representation Learning

### Can environmental dynamics be represented beyond a single task?

This current stage develops query-based representations of land-surface dynamics from heterogeneous, asynchronous, and incomplete Earth observation data.

<details class="research-details">
<summary>How this research is developing</summary>
<div class="research-details-body">
<h4>Framework</h4>
<p>My current work explores a query-based multimodal spatiotemporal representation-learning framework for Earth observation. The framework represents heterogeneous observations as multimodal tokens, augmented with modality, temporal, and spatial embeddings to preserve their source, acquisition time, and spatial context.</p>
<h4>Learning formulation</h4>
<p>A temporal query uses attention over the available observation tokens to infer a representation at a specified location and time. Filtering, forecasting, and smoothing can therefore be expressed within the same framework by changing the temporal relationship between the observations and the query, rather than constructing a separate model for each task. Training primarily uses self-supervised context–target prediction: a subset of observations is supplied as context, while withheld observations provide prediction targets.</p>
<h4>Current focus</h4>
<p>Preliminary experiments indicate that accurate reconstruction does not necessarily imply faithful representation of temporal dynamics. I am therefore focusing on improving temporal representation learning and extending the framework across modalities and datasets.</p>
</div>
</details>

[Research details →](projects/meteoste.qmd){.text-link}
:::

## Rice Leaf Area Index Retrieval

### Learning crop physiological information from multispectral imagery

This work connected multispectral observations with field measurements to retrieve a key physiological indicator of rice growth.

<details class="research-details">
<summary>Research overview</summary>
<div class="research-details-body">
<p>This research investigated how multispectral observations can be used to estimate rice leaf area index. It established my early work in remote-sensing feature extraction, machine-learning-based retrieval, and the interpretation of crop physiological variables from imagery.</p>
</div>
</details>

## Rice Growth and Zinc Dynamics Modeling

### Connecting crop growth, soil transport, and grain biofortification

This work linked crop growth, soil transport, and organ-level zinc translocation within a process-based modelling framework.

<details class="research-details">
<summary>Research overview</summary>
<div class="research-details-body">
<p>This work developed a process-based framework for representing zinc movement across the soil–plant–grain continuum. By coupling crop growth, soil water and solute transport, and organ-level zinc translocation, it shifted my research from empirical retrieval toward explicit modelling of environmental processes and their interactions.</p>
</div>
</details>

[Research details →](projects/rzdm.qmd){.text-link} · [Publication →](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compag.2026.112134){.text-link}
:::
:::

::: {.research-synthesis}
**Research trajectory:** retrieve crop states from imagery → model crop–environment processes → quantify multimodal information → learn spatial representations with limited supervision → develop transferable representations of environmentally driven spatiotemporal dynamics.
:::
